procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated September 25, 1953, of the Labour Appellate Tribunal of India, Calcutta in Miscellaneous Case No. C-112 of 1953.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Labour Appellate Tribunal dismissed the application of the appellant company.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Appeal by special leave from the judgment and order of the Labour Appellate Tribunal. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and set aside the decision of the Labour Appellate Tribunal.

directions: Permission be granted to the appellant to discharge ninety six temporary workmen.
The parties must bear their own costs throughout.

issue.issue_text: Whether the scope of an enquiry under s. 22 of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950, is to determine if a prima facie case is made out for the proposed discharge and if the employer has resorted to any unfair practice or victimisation.

facts: An employer sought permission from the Labour Appellate Tribunal under Section 22 of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950, to discharge several temporary employees.
The Labour Appellate Tribunal dismissed the employer's application, focusing its decision on a finding that the erection works for which the employees were hired had already been completed.
The employer appealed this decision to the Supreme Court, arguing that the Tribunal had not correctly understood the limited scope of an enquiry under Section 22.
law: The Supreme Court affirmed that the purpose of Section 22 of the 1950 Act (similar to Section 33 of the 1947 Act) is to protect workmen from victimisation by an employer while other industrial disputes are pending.
The Court cited its previous decision in *Atherton West & Co. Ltd. v. Suti Mill Mazdoor Union*, which established that the scope of an enquiry under such provisions is limited.

The legal principle is that the authority's role is not to fully adjudicate the merits of the discharge, but to determine two key things: 1) whether the employer has made out a *prima facie* case for the proposed discharge or dismissal, and 2) whether the employer is acting without improper motives and has not resorted to any unfair practice or victimisation.
application: The Supreme Court found that the Labour Appellate Tribunal had failed to apply this legal principle. Instead of determining if a prima facie case existed and checking for victimisation, the Tribunal had focused on a different, and not decisive, question regarding the completion of the erection works.
The Court stated that the real question was whether the employer had made a prima facie case for the proposed discharge and was acting in good faith.

Applying the correct legal standard to the facts, the Supreme Court conducted the enquiry itself. It found that the employer had successfully made out a prima facie case for the permission sought and that there was "no suggestion even of any unfair practice or victimisation."
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the issue, holding that the scope of an enquiry under Section 22 of the Act is indeed limited to determining whether a prima facie case for discharge has been made out and whether the employer's action is free from unfair practices or victimisation. Because the lower tribunal failed to conduct this specific enquiry, the Supreme Court set aside its decision.

issue.issue_text: Whether an Industrial Tribunal, while having the power to create new obligations or modify contracts, must exercise its discretion in accordance with well-recognised principles and cannot completely ignore existing agreements or obligations.

facts: The case involved an application by a company for permission to discharge temporary employees.
The Labour Appellate Tribunal dismissed the company's application.
The Supreme Court found that the Labour Appellate Tribunal did not decide the real question at issue, which was whether the workmen were in fact temporary employees.
Instead, the lower tribunal based its decision on an irrelevant finding about when certain erection works were completed.
law: An Industrial Tribunal is distinct from a regular court of law; unlike a court that can only enforce existing contracts, a Tribunal can create new obligations or modify contracts.
This power is granted to Tribunals to maintain industrial peace, protect legitimate trade union activities, and prevent unfair practices or victimisation.
However, this power is not absolute. The discretion of an Industrial Tribunal must be exercised in accordance with "well recognised principles."
A Tribunal cannot completely ignore an existing agreement or existing obligations "for no rhyme or reason whatsoever."
application: The Court found that the Labour Appellate Tribunal had failed to exercise its discretion according to well-recognised principles.
By not directing its mind to the real question (whether the employees were temporary) and instead focusing on an irrelevant point, the lower tribunal misused its discretion.
The Supreme Court characterized this failure as resulting in "manifest injustice," which justified its intervention.

The Court determined that the lower tribunal's failure to properly consider the application was a violation of the principle that its discretion must be exercised properly and in line with established procedures.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the principle that an Industrial Tribunal's power to create new obligations or modify contracts is not unlimited. It held that this discretion must be exercised in accordance with well-recognised principles and that a Tribunal cannot arbitrarily ignore existing agreements. The Court found that the lower tribunal had failed to do this by not addressing the central issue of the case, thereby misusing its discretion and justifying the reversal of its decision.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court can interfere with a decision of the Labour Appellate Tribunal under Article 136 of the Constitution when the Tribunal has not addressed the real question to be decided, leading to manifest injustice.

facts: The Labour Appellate Tribunal (LAT) was asked to decide on an application under section 22 of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950, for permission to discharge employees.

The real question to be decided was whether the company had a prima facie case for discharging the employees (i.e., were they temporary?) and whether the company was acting unfairly or engaging in victimisation.
Instead of deciding this question, the LAT focused on a different and somewhat irrelevant issue: the completion date of the erection works.
The LAT dismissed the company's application based on its finding on this irrelevant point, without ever determining if the employees were temporary or not.
law: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court has special powers to interfere with decisions of lower courts and tribunals.
The Supreme Court does not act as an ordinary court of appeal for decisions of Industrial Tribunals; there must be "special circumstances" to justify its interference.
The discretion granted to an Industrial Tribunal must be exercised in accordance with well-recognized principles and cannot be arbitrary.
A failure by a tribunal to direct its mind to the real question to be decided, which results in manifest injustice, can constitute "special circumstances".
application: The Court acknowledged the respondent's argument that it should not interfere with a tribunal's findings of fact or its discretionary decisions.
However, the Court found that the LAT had not actually made a finding on the key factual question of whether the employees were temporary.
The Court determined that the LAT failed to address the real legal question before it, which was to assess if a prima facie case for discharge existed without any unfair practice.
By basing its order on an irrelevant finding (the completion of erection works), the LAT failed to exercise its discretion according to established principles.

The Court held that this failure by the LAT to direct its mind to the real issue and the resulting order based on an irrelevant finding created "special circumstances" that resulted in "manifest injustice."
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that it could interfere with the Labour Appellate Tribunal's decision under Article 136. The Tribunal's failure to address the real question at issue and its reliance on an irrelevant finding constituted special circumstances that led to a manifest injustice, thereby justifying the exercise of the Court's special powers.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the scope of an enquiry under s. 22 of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950, is to determine if a prima facie case is made out for the proposed discharge and if the employer has resorted to any unfair practice or victimisation.
appellant_arguments: The completion of the erection works was a gradual process, and the workmen, who were temporary, became redundant as the work was completed.
The workmen's own schedule (Annexure A) supports the company's case that the erection work was completed gradually, with some finishing in 1952.

The Labour Appellate Tribunal's conclusion, based on a Director's report from July 1951, that all erection work was finished by the end of 1950 is a 'complete non sequitur' and ignores the gradual nature of the work's completion.
respondent_arguments: The erection work was completed towards the end of 1950, making the company's reason for discharge 'patently false'.
Many workmen were absorbed as permanent workers in other factories or in the maintenance section after the erection work.
The real reason for the proposed retrenchment is the company's desire to increase the workload and 'increase the rate of exploitation of its workmen', which constitutes an unfair practice.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an Industrial Tribunal, while having the power to create new obligations or modify contracts, must exercise its discretion in accordance with well-recognised principles and cannot completely ignore existing agreements or obligations.
appellant_arguments: The workmen were hired as temporary employees under specific terms of employment.
Under these terms, temporary employees could be moved from one work to another, and their employment in a production department for some time did not make them permanent.
respondent_arguments: The appointment forms containing the terms of temporary employment should be ignored because workmen were 'forced to sign' them under duress after a strike for the 'purpose of humiliating and terrorising them'.
Despite the forms, many workmen were later transferred as permanent workers to other factories or absorbed into permanent roles in the maintenance section.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court can interfere with a decision of the Labour Appellate Tribunal under Article 136 of the Constitution when the Tribunal has not addressed the real question to be decided, leading to manifest injustice.
appellant_arguments: The Labour Appellate Tribunal's conclusion regarding the completion of erection works was a 'complete non sequitur'.

The Tribunal completely ignored relevant circumstances, such as the terms of employment and the fact that enjoying some benefits of permanent employees does not confer permanent status on temporary workers.
respondent_arguments: The provided text does not contain the respondent's arguments on this specific issue.

cases.case_name: The Automobile Products of India Ltd. v. Rukmaji Bala
cases.principle: Section 22 of the Act confers on the Appellate Tribunal a special jurisdiction which is in the nature of original jurisdiction, and the Tribunal, being an authority of limited jurisdiction, must be confined to the exercise of such functions and powers as are actually conferred on it.

cases.case_name: Atherton West & Co. Ltd. v. Suti Mill Mazdoor Union
cases.principle: Though an Industrial Tribunal can create new obligations or modify contracts in the interests of industrial peace, its discretion has to be exercised in accordance with well recognised principles and it cannot ignore altogether an existing agreement or existing obligations.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An Industrial Tribunal has the authority to create new obligations or modify existing contracts in the interest of industrial peace, to protect trade union activities, and to prevent unfair practices or victimisation. However, this discretion is not absolute; it must be exercised in accordance with well-recognized principles and cannot be used to ignore existing agreements or obligations without a valid reason. The scope of an inquiry for permission to discharge a workman is to determine if a prima facie case has been made out and that the employer is not motivated by improper motives, unfair practice, or victimisation.
obiter: A question of interpretation of section 33 of the Industrial Disputes (Amendment and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1956 might have arisen if the case were remanded, but the court abstained from expressing any opinion on it.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court concluded that the Labour Appellate Tribunal had fundamentally erred by failing to conduct the proper inquiry required under section 22 of the 1950 Act. The Tribunal's duty was to determine whether the employer had made out a prima facie case for the proposed discharge and was not resorting to unfair practices or victimisation. Instead, the Tribunal based its decision on a single, irrelevant, and factually flawed finding regarding the completion date of erection works. This failure to address the real question at issue resulted in a manifest injustice, compelling the Supreme Court to intervene, set aside the decision, and grant the employer permission to discharge the temporary workmen.
legal_tests_applied: The scope of an enquiry under section 22 of the Act is to determine 'whether there was a prima facie case made out for the discharge or dismissal of the workman and the employer, his agent or manager was not actuated by any improper motives or did not resort to any unfair practice or victimisation in the matter of the proposed discharge or dismissal of the workman.'

The Supreme Court may exercise its special power under Article 136 of the Constitution when 'special circumstances exist... where the Labour Appellate Tribunal has not directed its mind to the real question to be decided on an application under section 22 of the Act and has passed an order on the basis of a somewhat irrelevant finding which has resulted in manifest injustice.'
policy_considerations: While an Industrial Tribunal may create new obligations or modify contracts in the interests of industrial peace, it cannot 'ignore altogether an existing agreement or existing obligations for no rhyme or reason whatsoever.'
The discretion which an Industrial Tribunal has must be exercised in accordance with well recognised principles.

The object of section 22 of the 1950 Act is to protect workmen involved in pending proceedings against victimisation and to ensure industrial peace by imposing a ban on the employer's ordinary right to alter conditions of service, a ban which can only be removed by permission from the relevant authority.
